samudra-manthan.name: Samudra Manthan (Churning of the Ocean)
aliases: Churning of the Ocean of Milk
samudra-manthan.description: The devas and asuras jointly churned the cosmic ocean, using Mount Mandara as the churning rod and the serpent Vasuki as the rope, to obtain amrita, the nectar of immortality. The episode yields the poison halahala, drunk by Shiva, and a series of treasures including Lakshmi, and ends with Vishnu as Mohini denying the nectar to the asuras.
samudra-manthan.story: Weakened, the gods allied with their rivals the asuras to churn the ocean for amrita. Mount Mandara was uprooted and set in the sea as the churning stick, and the serpent Vasuki was wound around it as the rope, the asuras holding the head and the gods the tail. When the mountain began to sink, Vishnu took the form of a great tortoise, Kurma, and bore it on his back. The first thing to rise was the deadly poison halahala, which threatened to burn the worlds until Shiva drank it and held it in his throat, which turned blue. Then arose the moon, the goddess Shri, the white horse Uchchaihshravas, the jewel Kaustubha, the wish-granting cow, the elephant Airavata, and finally Dhanvantari bearing the pot of amrita. When the asuras seized it, Vishnu appeared as the enchantress Mohini and served the nectar to the gods alone.
variations: The Ramayana and Mahabharata place the churning in the ordinary ocean (turned to milk by herbs in the Mahabharata); the Puranas name it the Ocean of Milk.
The Vishnu Purana ascribes the gods' weakness to Durvasa's curse on Indra; the Bhagavata names Bali as leader of the asuras.
The number and order of the treasures (ratnas) vary; later lists fix them at fourteen, sometimes including Alakshmi (Jyeshtha) as the first to emerge.
In the Ramayana Vishnu himself supports the mountain; the explicit Kurma avatar is elaborated in the Puranas.

daksha-yajna.name: Daksha Yajna
daksha-yajna.description: The Prajapati Daksha held a great sacrifice to which he did not invite Shiva, and in the Puranic versions his daughter Sati gave up her life in protest. Shiva's wrath, embodied in Virabhadra and Bhadrakali, destroyed the sacrifice before Daksha was restored and Shiva given his due share.
daksha-yajna.story: Daksha, a son of Brahma, bore a grudge against his son-in-law Shiva, whose ascetic ways he despised. He organised a grand sacrifice and invited all the gods except Shiva. Sati, Daksha's daughter and Shiva's wife, went uninvited to her father's house; insulted there, she gave up her body in the sacrificial fire through yogic power. Learning of her death, Shiva tore a lock of his matted hair and dashed it to the ground, and from it sprang Virabhadra, with Bhadrakali born of the Goddess's wrath. Their hosts overran the sacrifice: Bhaga lost his eyes, Pushan his teeth, Bhrigu his beard, and Daksha was beheaded. At Brahma's plea Shiva relented, restored the gods, and gave Daksha the head of a goat, and Daksha thereafter honoured Shiva with a share of every sacrifice.
sources: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 66 (Shiva's bow used at Daksha's sacrifice)
variations: Vedic precursor: Rudra, excluded from the gods' sacrifice, pierces it; Bhaga is blinded and Pushan loses his teeth (Taittiriya Samhita 2.6.8, Shatapatha and Gopatha Brahmanas).
In the Mahabharata Shiva destroys the sacrifice (sometimes himself, sometimes through Virabhadra) at Uma's distress; Sati's self-immolation belongs to the Puranas.
Later Shakta texts (Devi Bhagavata, Kalika Purana) have Shiva wander carrying Sati's corpse until Vishnu's discus divides it, the pieces founding the Shakti Pithas.
In the Mahabhagavata Purana Sati manifests the ten Mahavidyas to overcome Shiva's refusal to let her go.

ganga-descent.name: Descent of the Ganga (Gangavatarana)
ganga-descent.description: King Bhagiratha of the Ikshvaku line brought the celestial river Ganga down to earth to purify the ashes of his ancestors, the sixty thousand sons of Sagara burnt by the sage Kapila. Shiva caught the torrent in his matted locks to spare the earth its force.
ganga-descent.story: King Sagara of Ayodhya performed a horse sacrifice, but the horse vanished. His sixty thousand sons dug down into the earth searching for it and found it grazing beside the sage Kapila. Accusing him of theft, they rushed at him, and the sage reduced them to ashes with a glance. Sagara's grandson Anshuman recovered the horse and learned from Garuda that only the waters of the heavenly Ganga could redeem them. Anshuman and his son Dilipa died without success, but Dilipa's son Bhagiratha performed fierce austerities. Brahma granted the boon, but warned that only Shiva could bear the river's fall. Pleased by further penance, Shiva received Ganga in his matted hair, subdued her pride, and released her in streams. Bhagiratha led her across the land and down to the netherworld, where her waters washed the ashes and freed his ancestors.
variations: In the Ramayana Ganga is the elder daughter of Himavan and Mena; Vaishnava Puranas describe her as flowing from Vishnu's foot, washed by Brahma at the Vamana episode.
The sage Jahnu swallowed the river when it flooded his hermitage and released it from his ear, giving it the name Jahnavi.
In the Ramayana Indra steals the horse; some Puranas leave the thief unnamed or blame the asuras.

lingodbhava.name: Lingodbhava (the Pillar of Fire)
lingodbhava.description: During a dispute between Brahma and Vishnu over supremacy, Shiva appeared as an endless pillar of fire. Neither god could find its top or bottom, and they acknowledged Shiva as the supreme.
lingodbhava.story: Brahma and Vishnu once quarrelled over which of them was the greater creator. Suddenly a blazing column of fire appeared between them, stretching beyond sight in both directions. They agreed that whoever found its end would be supreme. Vishnu took the form of a boar and dug downward for ages, while Brahma became a swan and flew upward. Neither reached the limit. Vishnu returned and humbly admitted failure, but in several Puranic versions Brahma falsely claimed to have seen the top, citing as witness a ketaki flower that had been falling from the summit. Shiva then emerged from the pillar, revealing himself as the infinite source of both. He honoured Vishnu's honesty, and in the Shiva Purana cursed Brahma to receive no worship and the ketaki never to be offered to him.
variations: Brahma's lie and the ketaki flower appear in the Shiva and Skanda Puranas, not in the earliest (Vayu, Linga) accounts.
In the Shiva Purana Shiva sends Bhairava, who cuts off Brahma's fifth head for his falsehood.
Tamil tradition locates the pillar at Arunachala, celebrated in the Karthigai Deepam festival.
Some versions add the cow Surabhi as a second false witness.

tripura-dahana.name: Tripura Dahana (Burning of the Three Cities)
tripura-dahana.description: The asuras built three fortified cities of iron, silver and gold that could be destroyed only by a single arrow when they aligned. Shiva (Rudra), using a cosmic chariot and an arrow made of the gods themselves, burnt all three at once, earning the name Tripurantaka.
tripura-dahana.story: Three asura lords, sons of Taraka, won from Brahma the boon of three cities, one in heaven, one in the sky and one on earth, built by the architect Maya of gold, silver and iron. They could be destroyed only by a single arrow at the moment, once in a thousand years, when the cities aligned. Protected, the asuras oppressed the worlds, and the gods turned to Shiva. The gods fashioned for him a chariot from the whole cosmos: the earth was its body, the sun and moon its wheels, the Vedas its horses, and Brahma its charioteer. Vishnu became the arrow, with Agni at its point and Soma at its shaft. When the three cities came into line, Shiva loosed the arrow and burnt them all in an instant, and the asuras perished within them.
symbols: Three cities of gold, silver and iron
weapons: Pashupata / the arrow formed of Vishnu, Agni and Soma
tripura-dahana.abode: The three worlds (heaven, sky and earth)
variations: In the Brahmanas the gods conquer the asuras' three forts (of iron, silver and gold) by the power of the upasad offerings, with an arrow compounded of Agni, Soma and Vishnu.
The Mahabharata (Karna Parva) narrates the cosmic chariot, with Brahma as charioteer and the three sons of Taraka as the cities' lords.
In the Shiva and Linga Puranas Mount Meru becomes the bow and Vasuki the bowstring; Maya survives as a devotee of Shiva.
Some Puranas add that Vishnu first corrupted the asuras' virtue so that they became vulnerable, and that Ganesha had to be worshipped before the chariot could move.

kama-dahana.name: Kama Dahana (Burning of Kama)
kama-dahana.description: Kamadeva, god of desire, disturbed Shiva's meditation with his flower-arrows and was burnt to ashes by the fire of Shiva's third eye, becoming Ananga, the bodiless one. In the Puranic and Kalidasa tradition the gods sent him so that Shiva would wed Parvati and father a son to kill Tarakasura.
kama-dahana.story: The asura Tarakasura, invulnerable save to a son of Shiva, tormented the gods, but Shiva, grieving for Sati, sat absorbed in austerity on the Himalaya. Parvati, daughter of Himavan, served him daily in the hope of winning him. At Indra's urging, Kamadeva went with his wife Rati and his friend Vasanta, the spring, to awaken desire in Shiva. As Parvati approached, Kama drew his sugarcane bow and loosed a flower-arrow. Shiva felt a stir of longing, saw the archer, and opened his third eye; a flame leapt out and reduced Kama to ashes. Rati lamented bitterly, and Shiva, or the gods, promised that Kama would live again, bodiless or reborn. Parvati, realising that beauty alone could not win Shiva, turned to severe penance, and through it won him as husband.
kama-dahana.abode: Himalaya; the Ramayana places it at the Kamashrama near the Sarayu-Ganga confluence
sources: Shiva Purana, Rudra Samhita, Parvati Khanda
variations: In the Ramayana the story is brief: Kama struck Shiva during his austerities and was burnt, becoming bodiless (Ananga); Parvati and Taraka are not mentioned.
The Harivamsha, Vishnu and Bhagavata Puranas say Kama was reborn as Pradyumna, son of Krishna and Rukmini, and Rati as Mayavati.
In South India Holi is associated with the burning of Kama rather than Holika.

skanda-birth.name: Birth of Skanda and slaying of Taraka
skanda-birth.description: Shiva's fiery seed, too potent to be borne, passed through Agni and the Ganga and was nursed by the Krittikas, giving rise to the six-faced war-god Skanda (Kartikeya). Made general of the gods, he slew the asura Tarakasura.
skanda-birth.story: The gods needed a commander who could defeat the asuras, and above all Taraka, whom Brahma's boon made vulnerable only to a child of Shiva. Shiva's seed was so fiery that no one could bear it. Agni received it, and unable to hold it, cast it into the Ganga, who in turn deposited it among the reeds of the Sharavana on the mountainside. There a radiant child was born. The six Krittikas, the stars of the Pleiades, came to nurse him, and he grew six faces to drink from them all, earning the name Kartikeya. Only days old, he split the Krauncha mountain with his spear. Indra, fearing him, attacked and was defeated, then consecrated him as senapati, commander of the divine army. Leading the gods, Skanda slew Tarakasura with his spear, restoring heaven to the gods.
skanda-birth.abode: Sharavana on the Himalaya; Krauncha mountain
sources: Shiva Purana, Rudra Samhita, Kumara Khanda
variations: In the Mahabharata's Vana Parva Skanda is the son of Agni and Svaha, who took the forms of six of the seven Rishis' wives; Arundhati alone could not be imitated.
In the Vana Parva Skanda's chief foe is Mahisha; Taraka's slaying is prominent in the Shalya Parva, Kalidasa and the Puranas.
Tamil tradition (Kandha Puranam) makes the demon Surapadma his principal adversary and gives him a second wife, Valli.
Some versions have Parvati embrace the six infants, merging them into one child with six heads.

kurukshetra-war.name: Kurukshetra War
kurukshetra-war.description: The eighteen-day war fought at Kurukshetra between the Pandavas and their cousins the Kauravas for the throne of Hastinapura. It is the climax of the Mahabharata, ending in the near-annihilation of both armies and Yudhishthira's joyless victory.
kurukshetra-war.story: After thirteen years of exile, the Pandavas' claim to half the kingdom was refused by Duryodhana, and Krishna's embassy for peace failed. Eighteen armies gathered on the plain of Kurukshetra, seven for the Pandavas and eleven for the Kauravas. Krishna, sworn not to fight, served as Arjuna's charioteer. Bhishma commanded the Kauravas for ten days until Arjuna, sheltering behind Shikhandi, laid him on a bed of arrows. Drona then led; the young Abhimanyu died in his wheel formation, and Drona himself laid down his arms on hearing the false report of Ashwatthama's death and was beheaded by Dhrishtadyumna. Karna fell to Arjuna when his chariot wheel sank, Shalya to Yudhishthira, and on the last day Bhima shattered Duryodhana's thigh with his mace. That night Ashwatthama massacred the sleeping Pandava camp. Of the vast hosts, only a handful survived.
symbols: Arjuna's chariot with the ape banner
sources: Mahabharata, Bhishma, Drona, Karna, Shalya and Sauptika Parvas
variations: Regional and folk traditions add figures absent from the Sanskrit epic, such as Barbarika (Skanda Purana, Rajasthan) watching the war from a hilltop.
Tamil tradition relates Iravan's self-sacrifice to Kali before the war to ensure the Pandavas' victory.
The Critical Edition places some passages, such as Arjuna's hymn to Durga before the battle, in its appendices.

bhagavad-gita.name: The Bhagavad Gita discourse
bhagavad-gita.description: The dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna on the battlefield of Kurukshetra, just before the war, in which Krishna teaches the paths of duty, knowledge and devotion. Narrated by Sanjaya to Dhritarashtra, it forms eighteen chapters of the Bhishma Parva.
bhagavad-gita.story: As the two armies faced each other, Arjuna asked Krishna to drive his chariot between them. Seeing grandfather Bhishma, teacher Drona, cousins and friends arrayed to fight, he was overcome with grief, laid down his bow Gandiva and refused to fight. Krishna answered his despair with a teaching: the self is eternal and cannot be slain; one must do one's duty without attachment to its fruits; action offered to the divine binds no one. He explained the disciplines of action, knowledge, meditation and devotion. At Arjuna's request he revealed his universal form, in which Arjuna saw all creation and the warriors of both armies rushing into Krishna's mouths like moths into flame. Finally Krishna told him to surrender to him alone. Arjuna's doubts dispelled, he took up Gandiva again, ready to fight.
variations: The 700-verse vulgate is standard; a longer Kashmiri recension exists.
Commentators (Shankara, Ramanuja, Madhva and others) read the teaching through non-dual, qualified non-dual and dualist lenses.
The Anugita (Ashvamedhika Parva) is Krishna's later restatement when Arjuna says he has forgotten the teaching.

game-of-dice.name: The Game of Dice
game-of-dice.description: At Hastinapura, Yudhishthira lost his kingdom, his brothers, himself and Draupadi to Shakuni's loaded dice on Duryodhana's behalf. Draupadi's humiliation in the assembly hall, and a second game that sent the Pandavas into thirteen years of exile, set the course toward war.
game-of-dice.story: Envious of the Pandavas' wealth after the Rajasuya, Duryodhana, with his uncle Shakuni, persuaded Dhritarashtra to invite Yudhishthira to a game of dice. Bound by honour to accept, Yudhishthira played against Shakuni and lost his wealth, his kingdom, his brothers, himself and finally Draupadi. Dushasana dragged Draupadi by the hair into the assembly. She asked whether a man who had already lost himself could stake his wife; the elders fell silent, and only Vikarna and Vidura spoke for her. Karna ordered her stripped, but as Dushasana pulled at her garment, cloth kept appearing without end. Bhima vowed to break Duryodhana's thigh and drink Dushasana's blood. Terrified by evil omens, Dhritarashtra granted Draupadi boons and freed the Pandavas, but a second game cost them twelve years in the forest and a thirteenth in disguise.
sources: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva 43-72 (Dyuta and Anudyuta Parvas)
variations: In the Critical Edition the garment multiplies without Draupadi explicitly invoking Krishna; the vulgate and later devotional retellings have her pray to Krishna, who saves her.
Popular tradition holds that Shakuni's dice were made from his father's bones and obeyed his will; this is not in the Sanskrit epic.

draupadi-svayamvara.name: Draupadi's Svayamvara
draupadi-svayamvara.description: King Drupada of Panchala held a contest for his daughter Draupadi's hand: the suitor had to string a mighty bow and hit a target through a revolving device. Arjuna, disguised as a brahmin, won, and by Kunti's word Draupadi became the wife of all five Pandavas.
draupadi-svayamvara.story: Hoping that Arjuna, whom he believed dead, might still win his daughter, Drupada set a formidable test: string a great bow and shoot five arrows through a revolving aperture to strike a target above. Kings from across the land came, Duryodhana, Shishupala, Jarasandha, Shalya and others, and one after another failed. The Pandavas, living in disguise as brahmins since escaping the house of lac, sat among the priests. Arjuna rose, strung the bow in an instant and struck the target, and Draupadi garlanded him. The outraged kings attacked, but Arjuna and Bhima drove them off while Krishna, recognising his cousins, calmed the rest. Returning home, the brothers called out that they had brought alms; Kunti, unseeing, told them to share it equally. With Vyasa's sanction, Draupadi was wedded to all five brothers.
variations: In the vulgate Karna strings the bow but Draupadi refuses him as a charioteer's son; in the Critical Edition he fails by a hair's breadth and her refusal is not in the constituted text.
Later versions describe the target as a fish (matsya) on a revolving wheel, shot while looking at its reflection in water.
Vyasa justifies the polyandrous marriage by Draupadi's past life, in which she asked Shiva five times for a husband.

rajasuya.name: Yudhishthira's Rajasuya
rajasuya.description: The imperial consecration sacrifice performed by Yudhishthira at Indraprastha after his brothers subdued the kings of the four quarters. It was marked by the killing of Jarasandha beforehand, Krishna's slaying of Shishupala at the ceremony, and Duryodhana's humiliation in Maya's illusory hall.
rajasuya.story: Urged by Narada, who brought word that Pandu wished it, Yudhishthira resolved to perform the Rajasuya. Krishna warned that Jarasandha of Magadha, who held many kings captive, must first be removed; Bhima killed him in a wrestling match of many days. Arjuna, Bhima, Nakula and Sahadeva then conquered the four quarters and gathered tribute. At the sacrifice, with Vyasa and the great priests officiating, Bhishma advised that the first honour be given to Krishna. Shishupala of Chedi objected and heaped insults on Krishna, who had promised his mother to forgive a hundred offences; when the hundredth was passed, Krishna severed his head with the Sudarshana discus. Staying on in the wondrous hall built by Maya, Duryodhana mistook a crystal floor for water and water for floor, and was laughed at. His resentment led to the game of dice.
sources: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva 1-42 (Sabha, Mantra, Jarasandha-vadha, Digvijaya, Rajasuya, Arghabharana and Shishupala-vadha Parvas)
variations: The famous taunt by Draupadi, a blind man's son is blind, is not in the Critical Edition; there, Bhima and others laugh at Duryodhana.
Southern and vulgate recensions have Sahadeva send Ghatotkacha to Lanka to collect tribute from Vibhishana.

khandava-dahana.name: Burning of the Khandava Forest
khandava-dahana.description: To cure Agni of the surfeit caused by endless sacrificial butter, Krishna and Arjuna let him consume the Khandava forest, holding off Indra, who was protecting his friend the naga Takshaka. In return they received divine weapons, including the Gandiva bow and the Sudarshana discus.
khandava-dahana.story: Agni, sickened by the ghee of countless sacrifices, learned from Brahma that he could recover by devouring the Khandava forest, but every attempt was quenched by Indra's rains, for Indra's friend Takshaka lived there. Disguised as a brahmin, Agni approached Krishna and Arjuna on the banks of the Yamuna and asked for help. At their request he had Varuna give Arjuna the bow Gandiva, two inexhaustible quivers and a chariot with an ape banner, and Krishna the discus and the mace Kaumodaki. As the forest burned, the two warriors circled it, shooting down every creature that tried to escape and driving back Indra and the gods who attacked them. A heavenly voice told Indra that his friend Takshaka was away, and he withdrew. Only a few escaped, among them Takshaka's son Ashvasena and the asura architect Maya, whom Arjuna spared.
khandava-dahana.abode: Khandava forest (later Indraprastha), on the Yamuna
variations: The episode includes the sub-story of the Sharngaka birds, the sage Mandapala's children, whom Agni spared.
Some scholars read the episode as a memory of forest clearance for settlement and the displacement of naga peoples.

lanka-war.name: The War of Lanka
lanka-war.description: The war fought by Rama, Lakshmana and the vanara army against Ravana and the rakshasas of Lanka to rescue Sita. It ends with Ravana's death at Rama's hands, Vibhishana's coronation and Sita's ordeal by fire.
lanka-war.story: Having crossed the ocean by the bridge, Rama besieged Lanka with Sugriva's vanara hosts, joined by Ravana's brother Vibhishana. Angada went as envoy but Ravana refused to return Sita. In the fighting Nila slew the commander Prahasta, and Indrajit, striking invisibly, bound Rama and Lakshmana with serpent-arrows until Garuda freed them. Awakened from his long sleep, Kumbhakarna devoured vanaras until Rama cut him down. Indrajit felled Lakshmana, who was revived when Hanuman carried back a Himalayan peak bearing healing herbs; later Lakshmana killed Indrajit at the Nikumbhila shrine. Finally Ravana himself took the field. Rama, taught the Aditya Hridaya hymn by Agastya and riding Indra's chariot driven by Matali, fought him long, and slew him with the Brahmastra. Vibhishana was crowned king of Lanka, and Sita, after proving her purity through fire, was restored to Rama.
symbols: Sanjivani herbs and the mountain peak
variations: The Ahiravana (Mahiravana) episode, in which Hanuman rescues Rama and Lakshmana from the netherworld and meets his son Makardhvaja, is found in later and regional Ramayanas.
In the Adhyatma Ramayana and Ramcharitmanas the captive was a shadow Sita, and the fire ordeal restores the real Sita from Agni's keeping.
Bengali tradition (Krittivasi Ramayana) has Rama perform an untimely worship of Durga (akala bodhana) before the final battle.
Kalanemi's attempt to delay Hanuman on his way to the herbs appears in the Adhyatma Ramayana and Tulsidas.

sita-svayamvara.name: Sita's Svayamvara (breaking of Shiva's bow)
sita-svayamvara.description: At Mithila, Rama lifted, strung and broke the great bow of Shiva kept by King Janaka, winning Sita as his bride. The four sons of Dasharatha were then married to Sita, Urmila, Mandavi and Shrutakirti.
sita-svayamvara.story: Janaka of Mithila had found Sita in a furrow while ploughing and vowed to give her only to a man who could string the mighty bow of Shiva, entrusted to his ancestors after Shiva had wielded it at Daksha's sacrifice. Many kings had failed even to lift it. The sage Vishvamitra brought the young princes Rama and Lakshmana to Mithila. At his word, Rama drew the bow from its iron chest, lifted it lightly, strung it and drew it so hard that it broke with a thunderous crash. Janaka sent for Dasharatha, and in a great wedding Rama married Sita, Lakshmana married Urmila, and Bharata and Shatrughna married Mandavi and Shrutakirti, daughters of Janaka's brother Kushadhvaja. On the journey home, Parashurama confronted Rama over the broken bow and was humbled.
variations: In Valmiki there is no assembled svayamvara: Rama breaks the bow on a visit with Vishvamitra; later versions stage a contest before many kings.
Some later and folk versions have Ravana attend the contest and fail to lift the bow.
In the Ramcharitmanas Parashurama confronts Rama in the assembly itself; in Valmiki the meeting occurs on the road back to Ayodhya.
Janaka's queen is named Sunaina only in later texts.

rama-vanavasa.name: Rama's Exile
rama-vanavasa.description: On the eve of his consecration as heir, Rama was exiled to the forest for fourteen years when Queen Kaikeyi claimed two boons from King Dasharatha. Accompanied by Sita and Lakshmana, he wandered through hermitages from Chitrakuta to Panchavati while Bharata ruled in his name.
rama-vanavasa.story: Dasharatha announced that Rama would be made heir. Stirred by the maid Manthara, Queen Kaikeyi reminded the king of two boons he owed her and demanded that her son Bharata be crowned and Rama banished for fourteen years. Bound by his word, the king collapsed in grief, but Rama calmly accepted. Sita and Lakshmana insisted on going with him. Crossing the Ganga with the help of the Nishada chief Guha, they visited the sage Bharadvaja and settled at Chitrakuta. Dasharatha died of sorrow, recalling his curse for killing Shravana. Bharata refused the throne, came to the forest and begged Rama to return; when Rama would not break his father's word, Bharata carried his sandals back to rule as regent. The exiles moved south through the hermitages of Atri and Agastya to Panchavati.
sources: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya and Aranya Kandas
variations: Later tradition tells that Urmila slept through the fourteen years, taking on Lakshmana's sleep so that he could guard Rama; this is not in Valmiki.
Some retellings soften Kaikeyi's role, making her act at the gods' prompting so that Rama could fulfil his mission against Ravana.

sita-abduction.name: Abduction of Sita
sita-abduction.description: Provoked by Shurpanakha, Ravana used the rakshasa Maricha, disguised as a golden deer, to lure Rama and Lakshmana away from Panchavati, then carried Sita off to Lanka. The vulture Jatayu died trying to stop him.
sita-abduction.story: At Panchavati, Ravana's sister Shurpanakha tried to seduce Rama and, when rebuffed, attacked Sita; Lakshmana cut off her nose and ears. Rama then destroyed the rakshasa army of Khara and Dushana. Shurpanakha fled to Ravana and inflamed him with praise of Sita's beauty. Ravana compelled his uncle Maricha to take the form of a golden deer. Sita begged Rama to catch it; struck by his arrow, Maricha cried out in Rama's voice for help. Sita, frantic, sent Lakshmana after him. Ravana, disguised as a wandering ascetic, came to beg alms, revealed himself and carried Sita off in his aerial chariot. The aged vulture Jatayu fought him and fell with clipped wings. Sita dropped her ornaments to a group of vanaras below. The dying Jatayu told Rama what had happened, and the brothers began their search.
variations: The Lakshmana Rekha, the protective line Sita crossed, is absent from Valmiki and appears in later and popular retellings.
In the Adhyatma Ramayana and later texts Sita entrusts herself to Agni and a shadow Sita (Maya Sita), sometimes identified with Vedavati, is abducted.
In Valmiki Ravana seizes Sita by her hair and thighs; in Kamban he lifts the ground she stands on, leaving her untouched.

lanka-dahana.name: Burning of Lanka
aliases: Hanuman's leap and burning of Lanka
lanka-dahana.description: Hanuman leapt across the ocean, found Sita in Ravana's Ashoka grove and, after being captured and having his tail set alight, burnt the city of Lanka. The episode forms the heart of the Sundara Kanda.
lanka-dahana.story: Told by Sampati that Sita was in Lanka and urged on by Jambavan, Hanuman leapt across the ocean. On the way the mountain Mainaka rose to offer him rest, the serpent-mother Surasa tested him, and he killed the shadow-seizing Simhika. Overcoming the city's guardian goddess, he searched the palace, found Sita in the Ashoka grove guarded by rakshasis, and gave her Rama's ring. He then wrecked the grove and killed Ravana's son Akshayakumara. Indrajit bound him with the Brahmastra, and he let himself be led before Ravana. Vibhishana argued that an envoy must not be killed, so Ravana ordered his tail set on fire. Sita prayed that the fire be cool to him. Hanuman slipped his bonds, leapt from roof to roof and set Lanka ablaze, then, assured Sita was unharmed, flew back with her jewel for Rama.
variations: Tulsidas names the guardian of the city Lankini; in Valmiki she is the personified city, Lanka.
Regional traditions tell that Makardhvaja was born when a drop of Hanuman's sweat fell into the sea as he cooled his tail.

rama-setu.name: Building of Rama Setu
rama-setu.description: To bring his army across the ocean to Lanka, Rama had the vanara engineer Nala build a causeway of rocks and trees across the sea. The ocean god, humbled by Rama, promised to hold the materials afloat.
rama-setu.story: The vanara army reached the southern shore, but the ocean barred the way to Lanka. On Vibhishana's advice Rama lay on kusha grass for three days praying to the ocean for passage. When the ocean did not appear, Rama in anger aimed his arrows to dry up the sea. The ocean god rose before him, explained that he could not change his nature, but promised to bear up a bridge, and named the vanara Nala, son of the divine architect Vishvakarma, as able to build it. The vanaras uprooted trees and hurled boulders and mountain crags into the sea, and in five days Nala completed a causeway a hundred yojanas long. The army crossed over to Lanka, Rama and Lakshmana carried on the shoulders of Hanuman and Angada.
symbols: Rama's arrow aimed at the ocean
variations: Later retellings add that stones inscribed with Rama's name floated, and that Nala and Nila had been cursed so that anything they threw into water would float.
The tale of the squirrel carrying sand for the bridge, blessed with stripes by Rama, is a popular South Indian tradition.
Rama's worship of Shiva at Rameshvaram before or after the crossing is elaborated in later texts such as the Adhyatma Ramayana and Skanda Purana.

sarpa-satra.name: Janamejaya's Snake Sacrifice
sarpa-satra.description: King Janamejaya, to avenge his father Parikshit's death by the naga Takshaka, performed a sacrifice that drew serpents into the fire. It was halted by the young sage Astika, and during its sessions Vaishampayana first recited the Mahabharata.
sarpa-satra.story: Parikshit, cursed by a sage's son, died from the bite of the serpent Takshaka. When his son Janamejaya learned the truth, he resolved on a great snake sacrifice. As the priests chanted, serpents by thousands were drawn helplessly through the air into the fire, fulfilling an old curse of their mother Kadru. Takshaka fled to Indra for refuge, but the mantras dragged even Indra toward the flames, and he let Takshaka go. Just then the young brahmin Astika, son of the sage Jaratkaru and the naga woman Jaratkaru, sister of Vasuki, arrived and so pleased the king with his praise that Janamejaya granted him a boon. Astika asked that the sacrifice end, and Takshaka was saved in mid-air. During the long sessions of the rite, Vaishampayana, at Vyasa's bidding, recited the story of the Bharatas to the king.
variations: The Mahabharata is framed as recited twice: by Vaishampayana at the snake sacrifice, and later by Ugrashravas to the sages of the Naimisha forest.
Bengali and later Puranic tradition identify Astika's mother, the naga Jaratkaru, with the goddess Manasa.

three-strides.name: Vamana's Three Strides
three-strides.description: Vishnu, as the dwarf brahmin Vamana, asked the asura king Bali for as much land as he could cover in three steps, then grew to cosmic size and spanned the earth, sky and heaven, restoring the worlds to Indra. The striding Vishnu is praised already in the Rig Veda.
three-strides.story: Bali, grandson of Prahlada, had conquered the three worlds and driven Indra from heaven. Aditi, mother of the gods, grieved, and on Kashyapa's advice performed a vow, and Vishnu was born to her as Vamana, a dwarf brahmin boy. Vamana came to Bali's sacrifice and asked only for three paces of land. Bali's preceptor Shukracharya recognised Vishnu and warned him, but Bali would not break his word and poured the water of gift. At once the dwarf grew to fill the universe: with one step he covered the earth, with the second the heavens, and there was no place left for the third. Bali bowed and offered his own head. Pleased by his truthfulness, Vishnu sent him to rule Sutala in the netherworld and returned heaven to Indra.
three-strides.abode: Bali's sacrificial ground on the Narmada (Bhagavata); the three worlds
variations: In the Rig Veda Vishnu takes three strides across the worlds without any dwarf or Bali; the dwarf form (vamana) appears in the Shatapatha Brahmana, where the gods win as much land as the dwarf Vishnu can lie upon.
In the Bhagavata, Shukracharya tries to block the spout of the water-pot and loses an eye to a blade of grass.
In Kerala tradition, Mahabali was a just and beloved king allowed to visit his people once a year, celebrated at Onam.
Vaishnava Puranas say the Ganga issued from the water with which Brahma washed Vishnu's raised foot.

holika-dahan.name: Holika Dahan
holika-dahan.description: The demoness Holika, sister of Hiranyakashipu, sat in a fire holding the boy Prahlada, relying on her immunity to flame, but she was burnt while Prahlada, protected by his devotion to Vishnu, came out unharmed. The event is re-enacted with bonfires on the eve of Holi.
holika-dahan.story: Hiranyakashipu could not break his son Prahlada's devotion to Vishnu. He had the boy thrown from cliffs, trampled by elephants and bitten by serpents, but Prahlada survived every attempt. At last the king called on his sister Holika, who possessed a boon, or in some tellings a cloak, that made her immune to fire. A great pyre was built, and Holika sat in it with Prahlada on her lap. As the flames rose, Prahlada kept chanting the name of Vishnu. The protection passed from Holika to the boy: she was reduced to ashes, while Prahlada stepped from the fire unharmed. The triumph of devotion over malice is remembered each year by lighting bonfires on the full-moon night of Phalguna, the eve of the festival of colours.
holika-dahan.abode: Court of Hiranyakashipu (traditionally Multan, or Eranch in Uttar Pradesh)
sources: Vishnu Purana 1.17-20 (Prahlada's fire ordeal, without Holika)
variations: In the Vishnu and Bhagavata Puranas Prahlada survives fire among other trials, but Holika is not named; the Holika story is found in later Puranic and folk tradition.
Some versions say Holika's immunity came from a boon of Brahma, others from a shawl given by Agni that flew onto Prahlada.
The Bhavishya Purana links the Holi bonfire to a demoness named Dhundha; South Indian tradition links Holi to Kama Dahana.

mahishasura-vadha.name: Slaying of Mahishasura
aliases: Durga's victory over the buffalo demon
mahishasura-vadha.description: When the buffalo-demon Mahishasura conquered heaven, the combined radiance of the gods took form as the Goddess Durga, armed with their weapons, who slew him after a great battle. The episode forms the middle section of the Devi Mahatmya and is celebrated at Navaratri and Durga Puja.
mahishasura-vadha.story: Mahishasura, lord of the asuras, defeated the gods in a hundred-year war and seized Indra's throne. The gods, led by Brahma, went to Shiva and Vishnu, whose anger blazed forth as light; from the bodies of Indra and all the gods poured further radiance, which merged into a single luminous Goddess. Each god gave her a weapon: Shiva his trident, Vishnu his discus, Varuna a conch and noose, Agni a spear, Vayu a bow, Indra the thunderbolt and Airavata's bell, Yama his staff, Kubera a drinking cup, Vishvakarma an axe and armour, and Himavan a lion to ride. Her laughter shook the worlds. She destroyed Mahisha's generals and armies, then faced the shape-shifting demon, who became buffalo, lion, man and elephant. Drinking wine, she pinned him with her foot and, as he half-emerged from the buffalo, cut off his head.
mahishasura-vadha.abode: Heaven and earth; traditionally the Vindhya hills or Mysore (Chamundi Hill)
variations: In the Mahabharata (Vana Parva) Skanda, not the Goddess, slays Mahisha.
The Vamana Purana names the Goddess Katyayani, born in the hermitage of the sage Katyayana.
Later Puranas give Mahisha's origin as the son of the asura Rambha and a she-buffalo.
The Kalika Purana describes three killings of Mahisha in successive ages.

mausala.name: Mausala — End of the Yadavas
mausala.description: Thirty-six years after the Kurukshetra war, a curse brought on by a prank caused the Yadavas to slaughter one another with iron-hard reeds at Prabhasa. Balarama and Krishna then left the world, and Dvaraka was swallowed by the sea.
mausala.story: Young Yadavas dressed Samba as a pregnant woman and mockingly asked the visiting sages Vishvamitra, Kanva and Narada what she would bear. The sages cursed that she would give birth to an iron club that would destroy the race. Samba brought forth a club; it was ground to powder and cast into the sea, but it grew into reeds on the shore. Thirty-six years after the war, as Gandhari had cursed, the Yadavas went to Prabhasa and, drunk, quarrelled. Satyaki slew Kritavarma, and the fight became a massacre with the reeds, which turned to iron clubs in their hands. Pradyumna, Samba and Aniruddha perished. Balarama departed in yoga, a great serpent leaving his mouth. Krishna, lying in the forest, was struck in the foot by the hunter Jara's arrow and left the world. Arjuna led the women away as the sea swallowed Dvaraka.
variations: The Bhagavata Purana inserts Krishna's teaching to Uddhava (the Uddhava Gita) before the end.
Later tradition identifies the hunter Jara as a rebirth of Vali, repaying Rama's arrow from hiding.
Puranic reckoning dates the start of the Kali Yuga to Krishna's departure.

garuda-amrita.name: Garuda Steals the Amrita
garuda-amrita.description: To free his mother Vinata from slavery to her co-wife Kadru, the eagle Garuda flew to heaven, overcame the gods and seized the amrita. On the way he won boons from Vishnu and a pact with Indra, and the serpents lost the nectar they had bargained for.
garuda-amrita.story: Vinata and Kadru, wives of Kashyapa, wagered on the colour of the tail of the horse Uchchaihshravas; Kadru's serpent sons blackened it by clinging to it, and Vinata became Kadru's slave. Her son Garuda asked the serpents their price for her freedom, and they demanded the amrita. Garuda flew to heaven, scattered the gods who guarded it, passed through a whirling wheel of blades, killed the two serpents guarding the nectar and carried it off without tasting it. Vishnu, pleased by his restraint, granted him immortality and a place above his banner, and Garuda became his mount. Indra struck him with the thunderbolt, but Garuda dropped only a feather, and the two became friends. Garuda set the amrita on kusha grass before the serpents, freeing his mother; while they bathed, Indra took it back, and the serpents licking the grass split their tongues.
variations: In the Rig Veda an eagle or falcon (shyena) steals Soma from heaven for Indra; the Brahmanas tell of the wager between Kadru and Suparni, with the metre Gayatri in bird form fetching Soma.
The full Garuda-Vinata narrative is first found in the Mahabharata's Astika Parva.
Garuda's elder brother Aruna, born prematurely when Vinata broke his egg, cursed her to servitude.

vritra-vadha.name: Slaying of Vritra
vritra-vadha.description: Indra, strengthened by Soma, slew the serpent Vritra, who had enclosed the waters, with the thunderbolt fashioned by Tvashtr, releasing the rivers to flow to the sea. It is the central myth of the Rig Veda; later versions make Vritra a son of Tvashtr and have the vajra made from the sage Dadhichi's bones.
vritra-vadha.story: The serpent Vritra lay coiled upon the mountains, holding back the waters. Indra drank deeply of Soma from three bowls, took up the vajra that Tvashtr had fashioned for him and struck Vritra, the first-born of serpents. The waters rushed over the fallen body toward the sea like lowing cows, and Vritra's mother Danu, lying above him, was struck down too. In the Rig Veda, Indra's companions the Maruts and his friend Vishnu stand beside him. In later tellings Tvashtr created Vritra to avenge his son Vishvarupa, whom Indra had slain. No weapon could harm the demon, until Vishnu advised the gods to ask the sage Dadhichi for his bones, from which a new thunderbolt was made. Burdened by the sin of the killing, Indra hid, and Nahusha ruled heaven in his place.
vritra-vadha.abode: The mountains and the cosmic waters
variations: In the Rig Veda Vritra is a serpent or dragon (ahi) withholding the waters; in the Brahmanas and epics he is Tvashtr's creation to avenge Vishvarupa.
The Mahabharata and Bhagavata have the new vajra made from Dadhichi's bones; the Bhagavata portrays Vritra as a great devotee of Vishnu.
Some Rig Vedic hymns say all the gods deserted Indra except the Maruts or Vishnu.

mahaprasthana.name: Mahaprasthana — the Great Departure
mahaprasthana.description: After Krishna's death, the five Pandavas and Draupadi renounced the kingdom and walked toward the Himalaya and Mount Meru, followed by a dog. One by one they fell, until only Yudhishthira and the dog, Dharma in disguise, reached the gate of heaven.
mahaprasthana.story: Hearing of the Yadavas' end, Yudhishthira crowned Parikshit, entrusted him to Kripa and Yuyutsu, and set out with his brothers and Draupadi, a dog following them. At the sea Agni appeared and asked Arjuna to return the Gandiva, which he cast into the water for Varuna. Circling the land, they climbed into the Himalaya. Draupadi fell first, then Sahadeva, Nakula, Arjuna and Bhima; to Bhima's questions Yudhishthira named each one's fault. Indra came in his chariot to carry Yudhishthira to heaven, but he refused to enter without the faithful dog. The dog then revealed himself as Dharma, testing his son. In heaven Yudhishthira found Duryodhana enthroned and was shown his brothers in a hell, but it was an illusion; bathing in the heavenly Ganga, he shed his human body and joined his kin in glory.
variations: The epic names the dog as Dharma, Yudhishthira's divine father; Dharma is commonly identified with Yama (Dharmaraja).
In Uttarakhand tradition the route is associated with Badrinath and the Swargarohini peak.

govardhana-lila.name: Lifting of Govardhana
govardhana-lila.description: Krishna persuaded the cowherds of Vraja to worship Mount Govardhana instead of Indra; when the angry Indra sent a deluge, Krishna lifted the mountain and held it as an umbrella for seven days. Humbled, Indra consecrated Krishna as Govinda.
govardhana-lila.story: Each year the cowherds of Vraja offered a sacrifice to Indra, lord of rain. The boy Krishna asked his foster-father Nanda why they worshipped a distant god when their cattle lived from the grass of Mount Govardhana, and urged them to honour the mountain, the cows and the brahmins instead. They agreed, and offered their feast to the hill. Enraged, Indra unleashed torrential storm clouds on Vraja. The terrified cowherds and their herds ran to Krishna, who lifted Govardhana with one hand and held it aloft like an umbrella. For seven days and nights the whole village sheltered beneath it while the rain beat down in vain. At last Indra withdrew his clouds, came down on his elephant Airavata and bowed to Krishna, and with the cow of plenty consecrated him as Govinda, lord of cows.
symbols: Mount Govardhana held on one finger
sources: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (mentioned in Shishupala's taunts)
variations: In the Harivamsha Indra consecrates Krishna himself; in the Bhagavata the cow Surabhi bathes him with milk and names him Govinda.
Radha's presence at the event belongs to later devotional tradition (e.g. Gaudiya and Pushti Marga).
The episode is commemorated by Govardhana Puja and the Annakuta offering the day after Diwali.
